Orthopedics · published research

Bone density

Small human reports describe increased density at selected bone sites or around implants, while an eight-person study found no change at some measured sites or in bone markers.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small human reports describe increased density at selected bone sites or around implants, while an eight-person study found no change at some measured sites or in bone markers.

Summary of the Evidence

A narrow, outcome-based mapping identifies six PBM publications: four human reports and two animal experiments. They examine different contexts, including implant-site density and bone-density measures in people with osteoporosis or spinal-cord injury. This mapping does not treat all bone-repair studies as bone-density evidence, and the six publications do not represent one shared clinical outcome.

Human and clinical evidence

The human records include one randomized implant study, two other controlled or observational reports, and one case report. In an eight-person study of people with complete spinal-cord injury and osteoporosis, an 830-nm PBM protocol was associated with increased density at the proximal femur and forearm, while distal femur and tibia measurements and bone markers did not change (Mohammadzadeh et al. 2024). A small implant study reported increased local density and stability measures after treatment (Matys et al. 2019). A retrospective implant report also described increased CBCT density but lacked a concurrent control group (Luca et al. 2025). A case report is not independent comparative evidence.

Animal evidence

The narrow map includes one rat osteoporosis experiment and one rabbit distraction-osteogenesis study. They report changes in bone-density measures in preclinical models, not patient outcomes (Shokri et al. 2023).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified in this narrow mapping.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human studies use different settings and sites. The spinal-cord-injury study used an 830-nm near-infrared laser at 200 mW three times weekly for eight weeks, with reported fluences adjusted by target depth. Implant studies used localized red or near-infrared light near the surgical site. These procedures and measurements cannot be treated as one systemic bone-density regimen.

Interpretation

The reports show that selected density measures can change after PBM, but evidence is too small and varied to establish a clinically meaningful or general effect on bone density.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for clinically meaningful bone-density improvement across populations because the human evidence is small and procedure-specific
Publications and records6 unique titles in a narrow outcome-based PBM mapping

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The narrow mapping identifies four human publications, including one randomized implant study, two other controlled or observational reports, and one case report, alongside two animal experiments. The outcomes range from local implant-density measures to systemic bone density, so they do not establish one general effect. Independent controlled studies with clinically relevant follow-up are needed.
